task_2.title: Require Click 8 for Flask CLI
task_2.description: Flask 2.1.0 raises the minimum supported Click version to 8.0 and removes the prior compatibility path that allowed the CLI to run with Click 7 while emitting a deprecation warning. The CLI now relies on the standard Click 8 invocation behavior, and older Python environments also gain the declared importlib-metadata dependency.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to Flask 2.1.0 requires a Click 8.x-compatible CLI environment so Flask command-line usage works without legacy compatibility warnings or fallback behavior.

expectation.grounded: Flask 2.1.0 must declare `click >= 8.0` as a required dependency for CLI usage. The `flask` CLI entrypoint should run through Click's default `cli.main()` behavior instead of carrying the prior special handling for older Click versions. In Python environments earlier than 3.10, the distribution must also declare `importlib-metadata` as a dependency.
expectation.conceptual: After the upgrade, the command-line interface should only run in supported dependency environments and should behave according to the current supported Click runtime rather than maintaining backward-compatibility behavior for an older deprecated Click release.

constraints.grounded: Do not preserve support for Click 7.x or any deprecation-warning-only compatibility mode in Flask 2.1.0. The upgrade requirement should be expressed as a dependency contract and observable CLI behavior, without introducing separate user-visible fallback paths for unsupported Click versions.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should establish a clear supported CLI baseline instead of silently accommodating outdated dependencies. Users on unsupported dependency versions should be required to upgrade rather than relying on deprecated behavior.

behavior: Installing or resolving Flask 2.1.0 for CLI use now requires Click 8.0 or newer.
The Flask CLI no longer emits the previous deprecation warning path for running under Click 7.x, because that version is no longer supported.
The Flask CLI entrypoint now uses Click's standard main invocation behavior rather than an explicit forwarded argument list compatibility path.
Python environments earlier than 3.10 include `importlib-metadata` as a declared dependency.
acceptance_criteria: When a user upgrades to Flask 2.1.0, dependency resolution should require Click 8.0 or newer rather than allowing Click 7.x.
When the `flask` CLI is invoked in a supported environment, it should run through the current supported Click execution path without a deprecated Click-version warning mode.
When an environment is on Python earlier than 3.10, installing Flask 2.1.0 should include the declared `importlib-metadata` dependency.
When users operate the CLI after upgrading, observed behavior should align with the supported Click 8 runtime rather than legacy compatibility handling for older Click releases.

task_4.title: Extend deprecated Flask file-send parameter compatibility to 2.2
task_4.description: Flask 2.1.0 keeps supporting the pre-2.0 parameter names for file-sending helpers for one additional minor release. Applications may continue using the old names temporarily, but they should still see deprecation warnings and plan to migrate to the renamed parameters before removal in 2.2.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to Flask 2.1.0 preserves compatibility for applications still using the old `send_file` and `send_from_directory` parameter names introduced before Flask 2.0, while continuing to signal that these names are deprecated and scheduled for removal in a later release.

expectation.grounded: `send_file` must continue accepting the deprecated parameters `attachment_filename`, `cache_timeout`, and `add_etags` alongside their renamed counterparts `download_name`, `max_age`, and `etag`. `send_from_directory` must continue accepting the deprecated `filename` parameter alongside `path`. When a deprecated parameter name is used, Flask should emit a `DeprecationWarning` indicating that the old name remains deprecated and is now slated for removal in 2.2 rather than 2.1.
expectation.conceptual: Applications upgrading to Flask 2.1.0 should still work if they have not yet migrated to the renamed file-serving arguments, but the framework should clearly warn that the old argument names are transitional and will be removed in a future release.

constraints.grounded: This update should not change the functional behavior of `send_file` or `send_from_directory` beyond extending the deprecation window and updating the deprecation warning timeline. The renamed parameters remain the preferred public API, and use of the legacy names must still produce deprecation signals.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should preserve existing file-serving behavior and only relax the migration deadline. Backward compatibility should be temporary, not a reversal of the deprecation.

behavior: Using `attachment_filename` with `send_file` remains supported in Flask 2.1.0 and triggers a `DeprecationWarning` tied to migration to `download_name`.
Using `cache_timeout` with `send_file` remains supported in Flask 2.1.0 and triggers a `DeprecationWarning` tied to migration to `max_age`.
Using `add_etags` with `send_file` remains supported in Flask 2.1.0 and triggers a `DeprecationWarning` tied to migration to `etag`.
Using `filename` with `send_from_directory` remains supported in Flask 2.1.0 and triggers a `DeprecationWarning` tied to migration to `path`.
The deprecation warnings for these legacy parameter names must communicate that removal is deferred until Flask 2.2.
acceptance_criteria: When an application calls `send_file` with `attachment_filename`, it should still work in Flask 2.1.0 and emit a `DeprecationWarning` indicating migration to `download_name` and removal in 2.2.
When an application calls `send_file` with `cache_timeout`, it should still work in Flask 2.1.0 and emit a `DeprecationWarning` indicating migration to `max_age` and removal in 2.2.
When an application calls `send_file` with `add_etags`, it should still work in Flask 2.1.0 and emit a `DeprecationWarning` indicating migration to `etag` and removal in 2.2.
When an application calls `send_from_directory` with `filename`, it should still work in Flask 2.1.0 and emit a `DeprecationWarning` indicating migration to `path` and removal in 2.2.
When applications already use `download_name`, `max_age`, `etag`, and `path`, the upgrade should not introduce new behavior changes for those calls.

task_1.title: Raise the supported runtime baseline to Python 3.7+ and align async and JSON behavior with that baseline
task_1.description: Version 2.1.0 removes Python 3.6 support and stops carrying compatibility paths for runtimes that lack the standard-library features now guaranteed by Python 3.7+. JSON dataclass handling is treated as baseline behavior, and async execution depends on supported greenlet or PyPy versions rather than a legacy Flask-side ContextVar compatibility check.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2.1.0 treats Python 3.6 as unsupported, assumes Python 3.7+ standard-library capabilities for JSON serialization, and runs async features only within the supported greenlet or PyPy runtime matrix.

expectation.grounded: The upgrade should remove Python 3.6 compatibility expectations. `flask.json.JSONEncoder` and related JSON serialization behavior should assume the `dataclasses` module is present as part of the supported runtime. `Flask.async_to_sync` should continue to reject missing async support dependencies, but it should no longer perform a separate Flask-managed compatibility failure based on Werkzeug's fallback `ContextVar`; async execution is expected to run only on supported `contextvars` environments, including greenlet-based stacks that meet the documented minimum greenlet or PyPy version.
expectation.conceptual: After the upgrade, the library should target modern Python only. Dataclass-aware JSON behavior should be available as standard behavior on supported runtimes, and async features should work when the environment meets the supported async and greenlet requirements instead of depending on legacy compatibility shims.

constraints.grounded: Do not preserve Python 3.6-only compatibility branches or optional imports for standard-library features that are guaranteed on Python 3.7+. Keep the existing async dependency check in place, but do not reintroduce a Flask-specific runtime guard for Werkzeug's removed fallback `ContextVar` path. Treat unsupported greenlet or PyPy combinations as unsupported environments rather than a separately handled Flask compatibility mode.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must narrow the supported runtime matrix without changing the intended public behavior on supported environments. It should remove obsolete backward-compatibility handling while preserving normal JSON and async behavior for users on supported platforms.

behavior: Python 3.6 is no longer a supported runtime for this release.
Dataclass-aware JSON serialization is part of the baseline supported behavior instead of being conditionally available only on newer Python versions.

Async view adaptation through `Flask.async_to_sync` continues to require the async support dependency, but no longer raises a separate Flask-side compatibility error tied to Werkzeug's fallback `ContextVar` implementation.
Deployments using greenlet-based concurrency such as gevent or eventlet must satisfy the documented minimum greenlet or PyPy version for supported async context handling.
acceptance_criteria: When users upgrade to 2.1.0, Python 3.6 is treated as unsupported rather than partially compatible.
When supported Python versions serialize dataclass instances through Flask JSON facilities, the behavior is available without version-conditional fallback handling.
When async views or handlers are used without the required async support dependency, Flask still raises the existing async dependency failure.
When async features run on supported greenlet-based environments, Flask does not block execution because of a legacy `ContextVar` compatibility guard.
When users run unsupported greenlet or PyPy combinations, the release does not promise Flask-managed compatibility for those environments.

task_3.title: Remove reliance on Flask 2.0 deprecated APIs deleted in 2.1
task_3.description: Flask 2.1.0 removes several deprecated 2.0 compatibility paths and makes some previously warned-about behavior fail outright. The upgrade requirement is to stop relying on deleted helpers and config methods, remove implicit CLI app-factory assumptions, stop using removed JSON helper arguments, and ensure blueprint registrations use unique names.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the application and its supporting code are compatible with Flask 2.1.0 by removing reliance on deprecated APIs that were deleted, by making CLI app factories callable without implicit Flask-provided script context unless explicit factory arguments are supplied, and by preventing duplicate blueprint-name registration behavior that now fails instead of warning.

expectation.grounded: Code targeting Flask 2.1 must not rely on implicit `script_info` injection when Flask CLI resolves an app factory through `ScriptInfo.load_app`, `find_best_app`, or `find_app_by_string`; `Config.from_json` must no longer be part of the compatibility surface, with JSON config loading performed through `Config.from_file(..., load=json.load)` instead; `flask.json.dumps`, `dump`, `loads`, and `load` must be used without an `encoding` argument; imports and call sites must not depend on `flask.safe_join`, `flask.helpers.safe_join`, or `flask.helpers.total_seconds`; registering the same effective blueprint name more than once must be treated as invalid and require a distinct `name=` override; and test-client usage must no longer pass `as_tuple`, with request environ access taken from `response.request.environ`.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should preserve normal application behavior on Flask 2.1 while removing dependencies on APIs and compatibility shims that were only kept for older code. App loading, configuration loading, JSON handling, helper imports, blueprint registration, and client-side request inspection should all work through the supported 2.1 interfaces and fail early if old deprecated entry points are still used.

constraints.grounded: Valid zero-argument app factories and factories invoked with explicit arguments remain supported; only the implicit positional or keyword `script_info` injection is removed. Re-registering a blueprint remains allowed when each registration has a unique effective name. The 2.1 upgrade requirement should not assume that older `send_file` or `send_from_directory` alias parameters were removed here, because their deprecation window was extended.
constraints.conceptual: Keep existing supported usage working, but remove dependence on compatibility-only behavior. The change should tighten invalid cases without breaking correctly named blueprint reuse or correctly declared app factories.

behavior: Flask CLI app discovery now invokes discovered app factories directly and no longer passes `script_info` as either an implicit positional argument or a matching keyword argument.
`Config.from_json` is no longer available on the Flask config object.
`flask.json.dumps`, `dump`, `loads`, and `load` no longer consume an `encoding` parameter, so callers must use standard JSON string and file semantics instead of Flask-specific encoding adaptation.
`flask.helpers.safe_join` and the top-level `flask.safe_join` export are removed, and `flask.helpers.total_seconds` is removed.
Blueprint registration now raises `ValueError` whenever the computed registration name already exists, even if the existing entry refers to the same blueprint instance.
`FlaskClient.open` no longer supports the `as_tuple` parameter, and request environ access is exposed through `response.request.environ`.
acceptance_criteria: When Flask CLI loads an application from an app factory without explicit factory arguments, it should only succeed for factories that are valid without implicit `script_info`.
When application configuration is loaded from JSON on Flask 2.1, the runtime should not depend on a `Config.from_json` method being present.

When `flask.json` helper functions are called on Flask 2.1, they should be used without an `encoding` argument and should follow standard JSON text or UTF-8 handling instead of Flask-specific encoding conversion.

When application code imports or calls `safe_join` or `total_seconds`, it should rely on supported non-Flask compatibility APIs so that upgrading to Flask 2.1 does not produce missing import or missing attribute failures.
When a blueprint is registered more than once, each registration should have a unique effective name; reusing an existing name should fail with `ValueError`.
When code needs the request environ associated with a Flask test-client response, it should obtain it from `response.request.environ` and should not rely on tuple-style response returns.

task_6.title: Support async callables in copy_current_request_context
task_6.description: Flask 2.1.0 expands `copy_current_request_context` so it can wrap asynchronous functions as well as synchronous ones. Decorated async callables should execute through Flask's async compatibility layer while still receiving the copied request context, so callers get the completed function result instead of an unexecuted coroutine.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that functions decorated with `copy_current_request_context` work for both synchronous and asynchronous callables, preserving access to the current request context and returning normal application results when invoked.

expectation.grounded: `copy_current_request_context` must support decorating async functions in addition to sync functions. When the wrapped callable is async, invocation should run through the Flask app's async-to-sync execution path so the callable executes within the copied request context and yields its resolved result rather than exposing a raw coroutine to the caller.
expectation.conceptual: Applications should be able to use `copy_current_request_context` with async helpers the same way they use it with sync helpers. Calling the decorated function should execute it under the captured request context and produce the expected application value, regardless of whether the original function is synchronous or asynchronous.

constraints.grounded: Existing behavior for synchronous functions decorated with `copy_current_request_context` must remain unchanged. The copied request context must still be active while the wrapped callable runs, and async support must not require a separate decorator or different calling convention.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must add async compatibility without breaking current synchronous usage or changing how developers apply and call the decorator.

behavior: `copy_current_request_context` accepts async callables as valid decorator targets.
Invoking a decorated async callable executes it within the copied request context instead of returning an unexecuted coroutine object.
A decorated async callable can access request-scoped data the same way a decorated sync callable can.
Decorated synchronous callables continue to run with the same request-context behavior as before.
acceptance_criteria: When an async function is decorated with `copy_current_request_context` during an active request and later invoked, it should run to completion and return its resolved result.
When that decorated async function reads request-bound state, it should observe the captured request context while it executes.
When a synchronous function is decorated with `copy_current_request_context`, invoking it should continue to behave the same as in the previous release.
When application code uses `copy_current_request_context`, it should not need separate handling based on whether the wrapped callable is sync or async.

task_5.title: Deprecate RequestContext.g access
task_5.description: Flask 2.1.0 deprecates reading or assigning application globals through `RequestContext.g`. The `g` state remains available, but callers are expected to use the direct `g` proxy or `AppContext.g`, while deprecated request-context access now emits runtime deprecation warnings.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications upgrading to Flask 2.1.0 no longer rely on `RequestContext.g` as a supported way to read or replace request-scoped global state, while preserving the existing `g` behavior during the deprecation period.

expectation.grounded: In Flask 2.1.0, reading `RequestContext.g` must continue to return the current application context's `g` object, and assigning to `RequestContext.g` must continue to update that same object, but both operations are deprecated and should emit `DeprecationWarning`. Supported access should be through the direct `g` proxy or `AppContext.g`.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should preserve observable `g` state behavior for compatibility, but request-context access to that state must be treated as deprecated. Users should move to the supported `g` access paths and see a clear runtime deprecation signal if older request-context access is still used.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the current storage semantics of `g` in 2.1.0: deprecated `RequestContext.g` access must remain an alias to the application context's `g` object while warning, and supported access through `g` or `AppContext.g` must remain unaffected.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must not break current `g`-based behavior in this release, but it must clearly mark the request-context property as a temporary compatibility path rather than a supported long-term API.

behavior: Reading `RequestContext.g` continues to resolve to the current application context's `g` object.
Assigning through `RequestContext.g` continues to replace the current application context's `g` object.
Reading `RequestContext.g` emits a `DeprecationWarning` at runtime.
Assigning to `RequestContext.g` emits a `DeprecationWarning` at runtime.
Supported application code should use the direct `g` proxy or `AppContext.g` instead of `RequestContext.g`.
acceptance_criteria: When code reads `RequestContext.g` after upgrading to Flask 2.1.0, it should still receive the current application context's `g` object and emit a `DeprecationWarning`.
When code assigns a value to `RequestContext.g` after upgrading to Flask 2.1.0, the current application context's `g` should reflect that assignment and emit a `DeprecationWarning`.

When code accesses application globals through the supported direct `g` proxy or `AppContext.g`, it should observe the same application-scoped state without depending on the deprecated request-context property.
When existing code still uses `RequestContext.g` in Flask 2.1.0, its runtime behavior should remain compatible aside from the deprecation signal.

task_7.title: Restore Flask CLI plugin discovery without setuptools
task_7.description: Flask 2.1.0 updates CLI plugin command discovery to use import metadata instead of pkg_resources so extension commands continue to appear in minimal or hermetic environments where setuptools is not installed. The release also formalizes the metadata backport dependency for older Python versions and raises the Click baseline.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the Flask CLI continues to discover and expose plugin-provided subcommands during upgrade to 2.1.0 even when setuptools or pkg_resources is not installed, while keeping plugin command registration behavior consistent across supported Python versions.

expectation.grounded: The `flask` CLI must load commands registered in the `flask.commands` entry point group without requiring `pkg_resources` to be importable. Plugin command loading should not silently stop when `setuptools` is absent. On Python versions earlier than 3.10, equivalent entry point discovery support must remain available through the declared `importlib-metadata` dependency. The upgraded package also expects `click` 8.0 or newer.
expectation.conceptual: Users upgrading to Flask 2.1.0 should still see third-party CLI extension commands available in the `flask` command, including in stripped-down environments that do not bundle setuptools. The upgrade should preserve normal plugin command discovery behavior across supported Python versions.

constraints.grounded: Keep the existing entry-point-based plugin command model centered on the `flask.commands` group and preserve loaded command names and invocation behavior. Do not reintroduce a soft dependency on `pkg_resources`, and do not regress compatibility for supported Python releases that need metadata backport support. The dependency floor for Click must reflect 8.0+.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should change the dependency contract behind command discovery without changing how users register or invoke Flask CLI plugins. Existing working plugin commands should continue to behave the same, and environments that previously lost plugin commands due to missing setuptools should now work.

behavior: The `flask` CLI discovers plugin-provided subcommands from the `flask.commands` entry point group using Python import metadata rather than `pkg_resources`.
If `setuptools` or `pkg_resources` is unavailable, plugin command discovery is still performed instead of being skipped silently.
On Python versions below 3.10, the package declares `importlib-metadata` so entry point discovery remains available.
The upgraded release requires Click 8.0 or newer as part of its dependency contract.
acceptance_criteria: When a Flask extension registers a CLI command in the `flask.commands` entry point group, running the `flask` CLI should expose that command after upgrading to 2.1.0.
When Flask 2.1.0 is installed in an environment without setuptools or pkg_resources, plugin-provided CLI commands should still be discoverable and usable.
When Flask 2.1.0 is installed on Python versions earlier than 3.10, entry point based CLI plugin discovery should still function through the declared metadata support dependency.
When upgrading an environment that uses an older Click release, the dependency requirements should reflect that Flask 2.1.0 needs Click 8.0 or newer.

task_9.title: Add reloader exclude patterns to flask run
task_9.description: Flask 2.1.0 adds an `--exclude-patterns` option to `flask run` so developers can tell the development reloader to ignore matching file changes instead of restarting the server. This exposes underlying reloader support in a user-facing CLI workflow.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that `flask run` allows developers to provide file-pattern exclusions for the development reloader so changes to matching files do not restart the local server.

expectation.grounded: The `flask run` CLI must accept a new `--exclude-patterns` option. It must parse one or more patterns using the platform path separator, pass them through as `exclude_patterns` to the development server startup path, and ensure matching files are ignored by the reloader while non-matching changes continue to participate in reload behavior.
expectation.conceptual: Users starting the Flask development server should be able to declare ignore patterns for auto-reload. File changes that match those patterns should be skipped by the reloader, while ordinary watched files should still trigger reloads as usual.

constraints.grounded: The option must be optional, must coexist with existing `flask run` parameters such as reload, debugger, threading, SSL, and extra watched files, and must not change reload behavior when no exclude patterns are supplied. Only files matching the provided patterns should be excluded from triggering reloads.
constraints.conceptual: This addition should extend the development server configuration without altering existing startup options or default behavior. Ignoring files must be narrowly scoped to the patterns the user explicitly provides.

behavior: `flask run` exposes an `--exclude-patterns` CLI option for configuring reloader ignore rules.
The option accepts multiple patterns in a single value using the operating system's path separator.
Supplied patterns are forwarded into the server reloader configuration as exclude patterns.
Changes to files that match the configured patterns do not trigger an automatic reload.
Changes to files that do not match the configured patterns continue to trigger reloads under normal reloader behavior.
If `--exclude-patterns` is not provided, `flask run` behaves the same as before with respect to reloading.
acceptance_criteria: When a developer runs `flask run` with `--exclude-patterns` and the reloader is active, changing a file whose path matches one of the supplied patterns should not restart the development server.
When a developer runs `flask run` with `--exclude-patterns`, changing a watched file that does not match any supplied pattern should still restart the development server.
When multiple ignore patterns are supplied using the platform path separator, each supplied pattern should be honored by the reloader.
When `flask run` is started without `--exclude-patterns`, the development server's reload behavior should remain unchanged from prior behavior.

task_10.title: Preserve Click context across Flask debug reloads
task_10.description: Flask 2.1.0 fixes a `flask run` reloader issue where lazy-loaded app startup in the debugger could lose the active Click command context in the background loader thread. After the upgrade, app factories that rely on `click.get_current_context()` and data exposed through that context should continue to work after reloads, not only on the initial start.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications started through `flask run` keep the active CLI Click context available during lazy-loaded debug reloads so app-factory logic can continue reading command-scoped state after the reloader restarts.

expectation.grounded: When `flask run` uses the default lazy-loading debugger flow, application loading that happens in the background loader thread must preserve the current Click context. Calls to `click.get_current_context(silent=True)` during app creation should continue to return the active context after a reload instead of becoming unavailable, so context-backed state such as `ctx.obj` and `script_info` remains readable.
expectation.conceptual: Starting an app from the Flask CLI should behave consistently before and after an automatic debug reload. If application startup reads CLI context or values attached to it, those values should still be available after the process reloads.

constraints.grounded: The fix must be limited to preserving existing CLI context during background app loading and must not require callers to revert to deprecated app-factory argument patterns. If no current Click context exists, application loading should continue without introducing a new failure mode.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should restore lost CLI state during reloads without changing how applications start in normal cases or forcing a different integration pattern.

behavior: During `flask run` lazy loading, the active Click command context remains available inside the background loader thread.
After an automatic debug reload, `click.get_current_context(silent=True)` called from app-factory startup code no longer resolves to an absent context solely because loading moved to another thread.
CLI state stored on the current context, including data exposed through `ctx.obj` or `script_info`, remains accessible during app creation after reloads.
acceptance_criteria: When an application is started with `flask run` in debug mode and the reloader restarts it, app-factory code that calls `click.get_current_context(silent=True)` should still receive a current context after the restart.
When CLI options or setup logic attach values to the current Click context before app creation, the app factory should still be able to read those values after a lazy-loaded reload.

When application startup does not have an active Click context, the loader should continue to start or fail based on existing application behavior rather than because of the context-preservation change.

task_8.title: Preserve Custom FlaskClient Redirect Handling
task_8.description: Flask 2.1.0 fixes `FlaskClient.open` so applications that subclass the test client and override `open` can still follow redirects without runtime errors. The client now consistently normalizes supported request input forms and applies client-level environment defaults and preserved context across direct requests and redirect-generated requests.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that a custom `FlaskClient` subclass can override `open` to apply request defaults while `follow_redirects=True` continues to work without errors, including across internally generated redirect requests.

expectation.grounded: `flask.testing.FlaskClient.open` should continue accepting supported request inputs including `EnvironBuilder`, WSGI environ dictionaries, `BaseRequest` instances, and normal builder arguments. When a subclass overrides `open`, redirect resolution must not fail when `open` is re-entered with those request forms, and requests should consistently include the client's merged `environ_base` values and preserve-context state.
expectation.conceptual: Custom test clients should be able to centralize request customization in `open` without breaking redirect-following behavior. Redirected requests should behave like normal client requests and preserve the client's default request environment and context handling.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress existing `FlaskClient.open` usage for direct requests or non-redirect flows. Calls that pass an `EnvironBuilder`, environ dict, `BaseRequest`, or standard request arguments must still produce a normal test response, and `follow_redirects` must not require callers to avoid subclassing `FlaskClient.open`.
constraints.conceptual: Existing ways of issuing test-client requests should keep working. The fix should remove the redirect failure without changing the expected request API or forcing users to rewrite custom client subclasses.

behavior: A `FlaskClient` subclass that overrides `open` can issue requests with `follow_redirects=True` without raising a runtime error during redirect handling.
If redirect handling re-invokes `FlaskClient.open` with an `EnvironBuilder`, the request is accepted and processed as a normal redirected request.
When `FlaskClient.open` receives a WSGI environ dict or a `BaseRequest`, it dispatches the request with the client's environment defaults and preserved context applied.

When `FlaskClient.open` builds a request from normal arguments and keyword arguments, the same client-level environment defaults are applied consistently to both the initial request and any follow-up redirect requests.
acceptance_criteria: When an application sets `app.test_client_class` to a `FlaskClient` subclass that overrides `open` to inject default request data, calling `client.get(..., follow_redirects=True)` should return the final redirected response instead of failing during redirect processing.
When redirect processing internally passes an `EnvironBuilder` back into `FlaskClient.open`, the client should accept it and continue the redirect chain successfully.
When requests are issued through `FlaskClient.open` using an `EnvironBuilder`, environ dict, `BaseRequest`, or standard request arguments, the call should still yield a normal response object.
When client-level environment defaults or preserved request context are configured, they should apply consistently to both direct requests and redirect-followed requests.

task_11.title: Preserve HttpOnly When Clearing Session Cookies
task_11.description: Flask session clearing should preserve the configured HttpOnly protection on the expired session cookie that is sent when a modified session becomes empty, so cookie deletion does not weaken the cookie's security attributes.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that clearing a modified Flask session that becomes empty deletes the session cookie with the configured HttpOnly protection still applied.

expectation.grounded: When Flask saves a session through its standard session interface and the session is empty after being modified, the expired session cookie sent to delete the cookie must honor the configured HttpOnly setting from `SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY` in addition to the existing deletion attributes such as domain, path, secure, and same-site. This applies to the cookie-deletion response path for an empty modified session, not just normal session cookie creation.
expectation.conceptual: When an application clears its session, the browser should receive a deletion cookie that keeps the same HttpOnly security contract as the configured session cookie instead of dropping that protection during removal.

constraints.grounded: Only the deletion-cookie behavior for a modified session that ends up empty should change. Existing behavior for leaving an unmodified empty session untouched, for deciding whether a non-empty session cookie should be written, and for preserving the other configured cookie attributes during deletion must remain intact.
constraints.conceptual: The fix should be limited to preserving security metadata when removing a session cookie and should not otherwise alter when session cookies are created, skipped, or removed.

behavior: If a Flask session is modified and then becomes empty before the response is sent, Flask deletes the session cookie by sending an expired cookie that includes the configured HttpOnly attribute.
The deletion cookie continues to carry the same observable cookie-scoping and security attributes used for session cookie deletion, including domain, path, secure, and same-site settings.
If the session is empty and was not modified, Flask still returns without sending a deletion cookie.
acceptance_criteria: When `SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY` is enabled and a request modifies the session so that it ends empty, the response should include a session-cookie deletion header that is marked HttpOnly.
When a modified session becomes empty, the deletion cookie should preserve the configured domain, path, secure, and same-site behavior while also preserving HttpOnly.
When a session is already empty and not modified, Flask should not emit a session-cookie deletion header.

task_14.title: Preserve relative redirect Location headers by default
task_14.description: Flask 2.1.0 aligns redirect response behavior with Werkzeug so that default redirect Location headers stay relative instead of being expanded to absolute URLs with scheme and host. Applications upgrading from 2.0.3 should expect redirect consumers to receive path-only destinations unless an absolute URL is explicitly provided.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that after upgrading to Flask 2.1.0, redirect responses expose relative Location header values by default rather than automatically converting them into absolute URLs with scheme and domain.

expectation.grounded: Flask's Response should default `autocorrect_location_header` to disabled so redirect responses preserve relative `Location` values produced by Werkzeug or application redirects. Observable redirect targets should remain path-based such as `/login` or `/` unless the application explicitly provides an absolute URL.
expectation.conceptual: Redirects should now point to relative destinations by default. Callers that inspect redirect responses should see the same path the app intended to redirect to, without Flask adding the current scheme and host.

constraints.grounded: Do not rewrite relative redirect `Location` headers into absolute URLs during response generation. Preserve normal redirect semantics apart from the header format change, and do not change redirects that are already explicitly absolute.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should only change how redirect destinations are represented, not whether a redirect happens or where it ultimately leads. Existing explicit absolute redirects should continue to behave as explicit absolute redirects.

behavior: Redirect responses generated through Flask now keep relative `Location` header values instead of automatically prefixing the active scheme and host.
Path redirects such as those targeting the application root or another route should be surfaced to clients as relative paths.
This affects observable redirect headers at runtime for consumers that read `response.headers['Location']` or equivalent redirect metadata.
acceptance_criteria: When an endpoint returns a redirect to another application route using a relative destination, the response should expose a relative `Location` header such as `/target` rather than an absolute URL.
When Flask issues a redirect to the application root, the response should expose `/` as the `Location` header.
When a redirect destination is already absolute, the response should preserve that absolute destination instead of altering it.

task_13.title: Align Flask context manager exit typing with ExitStack
task_13.description: Flask 2.1.0 updates the public type annotations for context-manager-style `__exit__` methods so application, request, and testing client contexts are typed correctly when exiting without an exception and are compatible with `contextlib.ExitStack` and similar context manager protocols.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask context manager objects expose `__exit__` typing that allows normal context exits with no exception and can be used with standard context manager helpers such as `ExitStack` without type-checking incompatibilities.

expectation.grounded: The public `__exit__` signatures for `AppContext`, `RequestContext`, and `FlaskClient` should accept `None` for the exception type, exception instance, and traceback parameters to match normal context manager semantics. These objects should remain valid `AbstractContextManager`-style values for static type checkers when passed to `contextlib.ExitStack.enter_context` or equivalent APIs.
expectation.conceptual: Flask context managers should be typed the same way Python context managers actually behave: on a clean exit, no exception information is present, and standard context-manager utilities should recognize these objects as compatible.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the runtime exit behavior of `AppContext`, `RequestContext`, or `FlaskClient`. Their cleanup semantics and non-suppressing `__exit__` contract should remain unchanged; only the accepted typing of the exception-related inputs is broadened to include normal no-exception exits.
constraints.conceptual: This upgrade must improve type compatibility without altering how Flask contexts enter, clean up, or propagate exceptions at runtime.

behavior: `AppContext.__exit__` accepts the absence of exception information in its public typing, including normal exits where all exception-related arguments are `None`.
`RequestContext.__exit__` accepts the absence of exception information in its public typing, including normal exits where all exception-related arguments are `None`.
`FlaskClient.__exit__` accepts the absence of exception information in its public typing, including normal exits where all exception-related arguments are `None`.
Static type checkers should treat these Flask context manager objects as compatible with standard context manager protocols that permit `None` exception arguments.
No new runtime behavior is introduced; the change affects typing compatibility rather than execution flow.
acceptance_criteria: When a developer uses `app.app_context()` with `contextlib.ExitStack.enter_context`, supported static type checkers should no longer report a `__exit__` signature incompatibility caused by missing support for `None` exception arguments.
When a developer uses a Flask request context with standard context manager utilities, its public typing should allow clean exits where exception type, value, and traceback are absent.
When a developer uses `FlaskClient` as a context manager, its public typing should allow clean exits where exception type, value, and traceback are absent.
When these context managers are used at runtime, their existing cleanup behavior and exception propagation behavior should remain unchanged.

task_12.title: Relax error handler typing for precise exception annotations
task_12.description: Flask 2.1.0 relaxes the typing of error handler registration so applications can annotate handlers with the specific exception class they handle and can reuse the same handler across multiple registrations without static typing conflicts. The change is intended to improve developer-facing type behavior without changing runtime error handling semantics.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask error handler registration supports handlers typed to the specific exception they handle, and allows the same handler function to be registered for multiple exceptions without type-checking conflicts.

expectation.grounded: The public error handler registration APIs, including `errorhandler`, `register_error_handler`, and blueprint-level app error handler registration, should accept `ErrorHandlerCallable` values whose argument type is more specific than `Exception`. A handler registered for a given exception class should be valid when its parameter is annotated with that exact exception subclass, and the same callable should remain valid when decorated or registered multiple times for different exception classes. Registered handlers must continue to return Flask's normal `ResponseReturnValue` shapes.
expectation.conceptual: Applications should be able to declare error handlers using precise exception annotations instead of falling back to a generic `Exception` parameter, and they should be able to reuse one handler across multiple error registrations without typing friction. This should improve editor and type-checker support while preserving existing runtime behavior.

constraints.grounded: Registration by HTTP status code or exception class must continue to work through the existing public APIs. Relaxing the typing of `ErrorHandlerCallable` must not change how handlers are stored, selected, or invoked at runtime, and it must not restrict valid Flask response return types from error handlers.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should broaden what is accepted by static typing, not change how error handlers behave in production. Existing error handler registration patterns and response behavior must remain compatible.

behavior: A handler passed to `errorhandler` may annotate its error parameter with the concrete exception class being registered instead of a generic `Exception` type.
A handler passed to `register_error_handler` is treated with the same relaxed typing as decorator-based registration.
Blueprint-level application error handler registration accepts the same relaxed handler typing as app-level registration.
The same handler callable can be registered for multiple exceptions without the type system forcing a single generic exception parameter.
Error handlers continue to be modeled as callables that accept an error object and return any standard Flask response return value.
acceptance_criteria: When an application registers an error handler for a specific exception class, it should be valid for the handler parameter to use that same exception subclass annotation.
When the same handler function is registered for multiple exception classes, the registrations should remain valid from a typing perspective.
When an error handler is registered through either decorator-based or direct registration APIs, it should accept the same range of precise handler type annotations.
When existing code registers handlers by status code or exception class, it should continue to behave the same at runtime after the upgrade.
When an error handler returns any standard Flask response return value, that return contract should remain unchanged by the typing update.

task_15.title: Add prefixed environment config loading
task_15.description: Flask 2.1.0 adds a new configuration-loading entry point that reads environment variables with a chosen prefix, converts values to structured types by default, and supports nested dictionary updates. This allows applications upgrading from 2.0.3 to populate config from environment-based deployment settings without manually parsing strings.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications can load configuration from environment variables that use a dedicated prefix, with automatic structured value parsing and support for nested configuration keys.

expectation.grounded: Expose `Config.from_prefixed_env()` as a public config loader. By default it should read environment variables beginning with `FLASK_`, strip that prefix before storing the config key, and allow callers to provide another prefix. Each matching value should be passed through the `loads` callable, which defaults to JSON parsing, and if that conversion raises an error the original string value should be kept. Keys containing `__` should be interpreted as nested dictionary paths, creating missing intermediate dictionaries as needed. The loader should process matching environment variables in sorted order and report success with a truthy result.
expectation.conceptual: Applications should be able to initialize configuration directly from namespaced environment variables instead of only from files or manual string handling. Matching values should load as structured data when possible, nested settings should be expressible through the variable name, and malformed structured input should degrade to plain strings instead of breaking configuration loading.

constraints.grounded: Only environment variables with the selected prefix followed by an underscore should be imported. Loading should not fail solely because value deserialization fails; in that case the value remains a string. Existing config entries should remain untouched unless a loaded variable targets that same key or nested key path. Nested-path loading should create missing dictionary levels rather than requiring them to exist ahead of time.
constraints.conceptual: The feature should be isolated to an explicit environment-variable namespace, avoid surprising failures on ordinary string values, and preserve unrelated configuration state while applying only the settings that were explicitly provided through the chosen prefix.

behavior: A new `Config.from_prefixed_env()` API loads configuration values from environment variables using `FLASK_` as the default namespace prefix.
The loader accepts a custom prefix so applications can read from another namespaced set of environment variables.
Matching values are converted through a configurable loader function, with JSON decoding as the default behavior for booleans, numbers, lists, objects, and other valid JSON values.
If value conversion raises an error, the corresponding config entry is still loaded as its original string instead of aborting the load.
Environment variable names that contain `__` map to nested dictionary updates within the config, and any missing intermediate dictionaries are created automatically.
Matching variables are applied in sorted environment-variable order, providing deterministic load behavior when multiple prefixed values are present.
acceptance_criteria: When an application calls `Config.from_prefixed_env()` with no arguments, it should import only environment variables whose names start with `FLASK_` and store them under config keys with that prefix removed.
When a matching environment variable contains valid JSON such as a boolean, number, list, or object, the resulting config value should be the parsed structured value rather than a raw string.
When a matching environment variable contains a value that the active `loads` function cannot parse, configuration loading should still succeed and the config value should remain the original string.
When `Config.from_prefixed_env()` is called with a custom prefix, it should load from that namespace instead of the default `FLASK_` namespace.
When a matching environment variable name uses `__` separators, the loader should place the value into nested dictionaries and create any missing intermediate dictionary levels automatically.
When matching and non-matching environment variables coexist, only the matching prefixed variables should affect the config.
